slides.title: Real-world compressors: when, where, why
slides.body:
**Practical compression** balances: ratio, speed, memory, parallelism, format compatibility, licensing.

**General-purpose compressors**:
• **gzip (DEFLATE)**: 1992, RFC 1951. LZ77 + Huffman. Ubiquitous (web, Linux, packages). Mid-ratio, fast.
• **bzip2**: 1996. BWT + RLE + Huffman. Better ratio than gzip; slower.
• **xz (LZMA2)**: 2009. LZ77 variant + range coding. High ratio; slower than gzip; default for Linux kernel + Arch packages.
• **zstd**: 2015 Facebook. LZ77 + ANS. Fast + high-ratio. Becoming default in many: Linux kernel modules, btrfs, ZFS, Cloudflare.
• **brotli**: 2015 Google. LZ77 + context modeling + Huffman. Web (HTTP Content-Encoding: br); ~20% better than gzip for HTML/JS/CSS.
• **LZ4**: 2011. Fast LZ77 variant. Highest speed; modest ratio. Used in: compression for SQL Server, ZFS, Linux kernel boot.
• **Snappy / Snappy-frame**: Google 2011. Fast LZ77. Used in: BigTable, Hadoop, Lucene.

**Specialized**:
- **JPEG, MP3, etc.** (lossy media; covered earlier).
- **PNG**: lossless image; uses DEFLATE.
- **FLAC**: lossless audio.
- **Parquet, ORC** (database file formats): combine columnar + run-length + dictionary + Snappy/zstd compression.
- **Bloom filters + similar**: lossy sketches for set membership.

**Trade-offs**:
- Speed: LZ4 > Snappy > zstd > gzip > brotli > bzip2 > xz.
- Ratio: xz > brotli > zstd-max > bzip2 > gzip > zstd-1 > LZ4 > Snappy.
- Memory: xz, brotli need most; LZ4 + gzip least.
- Parallelism: zstd, xz, pigz (parallel gzip), pixz (parallel xz) support multi-threaded.

**Modern trend**: zstd increasingly default — combines high ratio + fast decode + good parallelism + permissive license.

slides.title: Block sizes, dictionaries, + parallelism
slides.body:
**Block size** matters for compression:
- Small blocks (~16 KB gzip): low memory + fast random access; lower ratio.
- Large blocks (~MB xz): high ratio; high memory; slow seek.
- zstd: ~4 MB default; adjustable.

**Dictionary compression**: pre-trained dictionary of common patterns. Decompressor must have same. Used for: small messages (e.g., HTTP headers, log lines, message-queue payloads).
- zstd: native dictionary support; train on representative samples.
- gzip: limited.
- Effectiveness: small messages (~500 bytes) often see 2-5× extra ratio.

**Parallel compression**:
- pigz (parallel gzip): independent blocks; near-linear scaling.
- xz: parallel mode.
- zstd: native multi-thread.
- Limitation: independent blocks → small ratio penalty; not all formats allow.

**Streaming compression**:
- All formats support, but block boundaries affect ratio.
- gzip streaming: emit on each input flush.
- Modern: zstd long-range mode (LDM) for streaming many GB.

**Random access** (decompress fragments without full scan):
- Most formats don't support natively.
- Solutions: index files (e.g., bgzip + tabix for genomic data), random-access zstd, lz4-frame.

**Compression as service**:
- HTTP Content-Encoding: gzip, br (brotli), zstd (since 2018).
- TCP-level: rarely; usually app-level.
- Cloud storage: S3 + GCS + Azure all offer + recommend compression.
- CDN: CloudFront + Cloudflare auto-compress text content.

**Storage compression**:
- File systems: btrfs + ZFS + XFS support transparent zstd or LZ4.
- Databases: PostgreSQL + MySQL support compression at table/page/column level.
- Time-series (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB): heavy use of compression + delta encoding.
- Log archival: zstd typically; gzip for compat.

slides.title: Compression in databases + streaming
slides.body:
**Column-oriented databases** (Parquet, ORC, Apache Arrow, ClickHouse, DuckDB, BigQuery) combine multiple compression techniques per column:

1. **Dictionary encoding**: replace strings with small integer IDs; saves space for low-cardinality columns.
2. **Run-length encoding (RLE)**: store repeating sequences as (value, count).
3. **Delta encoding**: store differences between consecutive values; small for monotonic.
4. **Bit-packing**: use minimum bits per value (16-bit ints in 12 bits if max value < 4096).
5. **General-purpose**: gzip, zstd, Snappy on top of all above.

Result: 10-100× compression vs raw row-oriented storage; analytic queries scan less data.

**Time-series-specific** (Prometheus, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB):
- Gorilla compression (Facebook 2015): variable-length encoding of double values; ~12 bytes → ~1-2 bytes typical.
- Delta + delta-of-delta for timestamps + monotonic counters.
- Combined: 10-50× compression typical.

**Log streaming**:
- Kafka + Pulsar + Kinesis: compression per batch.
- Log aggregators (Loki, Splunk, Datadog): heavy use of compression + sketches.

**Web + CDN**:
- Brotli for HTML/JS/CSS — ~20% better than gzip; widely supported.
- HTTP/3 (QUIC): per-request compression possibilities.
- Image CDNs (Cloudinary, Imgix): on-the-fly format conversion to AVIF/WebP.

**Container + image registries**:
- Docker uses gzip + zstd (--compression-mode zstd:chunked).
- Layered storage relies on compression for download speed.

**ML model serialization**:
- HuggingFace safetensors: no compression by default (compression breaks zero-copy memory mapping).
- ONNX: compression optional.
- Trade-off: smaller files vs decompression overhead.
- Quantization (int8, int4) is a primary 'compression' for ML models.

**Crypto + secure compression**:
- CRIME, BREACH attacks (2012, 2013): TLS + gzip-compression timing leaks. Mitigated via TLS-level controls.

question.question: Choose the right compressor for a use case

steps.prompt: Need: log files archived to S3; mainly stored, rarely retrieved.
steps.reveal: **xz / LZMA**: highest ratio at slow speed. S3 storage costs > compression time for cold archives. Modern alternative: zstd at level 19+ for similar ratio + faster decompress.

steps.prompt: Need: HTTP web pages from API; high request volume.
steps.reveal: **Brotli** (text-tuned; 20% better than gzip for HTML/JS/CSS) or **zstd** (general; web support growing). Both 2-3× faster decompress than gzip + better ratio. Browser support: Chrome + Firefox + Safari + Edge support both natively.

steps.prompt: Need: container image layers stored in registry.
steps.reveal: **zstd:chunked**: latest Docker + OCI default. Combines high ratio + fast decompression + parallel + supports lazy / chunked download. Replacing gzip standard. **gzip** for compat with old tooling.

steps.prompt: Need: real-time log streaming with low latency.
steps.reveal: **LZ4** or **Snappy**: very fast compress + decompress (multi-GB/s per core). Lower ratio (~2× vs gzip's 3×). Kafka + ClickHouse + log aggregators use these for hot streams.

steps.prompt: Need: scientific dataset (genomics, climate) with 10 TB.
steps.reveal: Multi-layered approach: domain-specific (delta encoding, Gorilla for time series, BCF/CRAM for genomics) + general-purpose (zstd or xz) on top. Indexed formats (HDF5, bgzip/tabix for genomic) allow random access. ML-based compression emerging for specialty (e.g., Cramore for genomic, climate-data-specific neural compression).

question.question: Order these compressors by *decompression speed* (fastest to slowest, on similar text).
question.explanation:
Decompression speed (approximate, MB/sec per core):
• **LZ4**: ~3-5 GB/sec; fastest.
• **Snappy**: ~2-3 GB/sec.
• **zstd (any level)**: ~1-2 GB/sec (slightly faster at level 1).
• **gzip**: ~300-500 MB/sec.
• **Brotli**: ~200-400 MB/sec; depends on level.
• **xz / LZMA**: ~100-200 MB/sec; slowest.

Decompression speed is what matters for read-heavy workloads (most apps + databases + CDNs read more than they compress). Compression speed inverted (slower for higher ratio). zstd's sweet spot: faster compression than gzip + similar/better ratio + multi-thread.

question.question: Why has zstd become the de facto default for many modern compressed workloads (Linux kernel modules, Docker images, ZFS, btrfs, Cloudflare HTTP)?
options: zstd combines: (1) high ratio (close to xz at high levels, similar to brotli); (2) fast compression (5-10× gzip); (3) very fast decompression (~1.5-2 GB/sec per core); (4) excellent multi-threading; (5) native dictionary support for small messages; (6) permissive BSD license; (7) wide format support including streaming + random-access. Combined: better than gzip + xz + brotli for most workloads. Backed by Facebook + actively developed; integrated into Linux kernel + Docker + most Linux distros.
question.explanation:
**zstd ascent (Facebook 2015 → de-facto default 2020s)**:

*Design goals* (Yann Collet, 2015):
- Better ratio than gzip at similar speed.
- Better speed than xz at similar ratio.
- Multi-threaded for both compression + decompression.
- Streaming support.
- Free/open-source.

*Technical decisions*:
- **LZ77** for matching (proven; well-understood).
- **Finite State Entropy (FSE)** / **tANS** for entropy coding (entropy-optimal at Huffman-like speed).
- **Compression levels 1-22**: span from LZ4-like speed to xz-like ratio.
- **Dictionary compression**: 10-100× compression for small messages.
- **Skipped frames**: small headers; random access feasible.
- **Streaming + frame format**: supports gigabyte-level streams.

*Performance (level 3 default)*:
- Compression: ~500 MB/sec/core (vs gzip ~100 MB/sec).
- Decompression: ~1.5 GB/sec/core (vs gzip ~400 MB/sec).
- Ratio: similar to gzip-6.
- High-ratio mode (level 19-22): ratio close to xz; slower.

*Adoption timeline*:
- 2015: initial Facebook release.
- 2017: Linux kernel module compression option.
- 2019: Cloudflare adopted for HTTP.
- 2020: ZFS native support.
- 2021: btrfs default option.
- 2022: Docker / OCI zstd:chunked default for new images.
- 2023: HTTP Content-Encoding: zstd added to RFC.
- 2024: most Linux distros default-include zstd.

*Why broader adoption than xz + brotli*:
- xz: high ratio but very slow decompression; bad for high-throughput.
- brotli: web-optimized; less general-purpose; not as fast at archive levels.
- gzip: legacy + universal; slowly being replaced.
- LZ4: too low ratio for general use; specialized for in-memory.

*Future*:
- zstd-tail-end-of-distribution improvements: long-range mode (LDM) for huge files.
- ML-augmented dictionaries.
- Hardware acceleration: ARM + Intel + AMD all have zstd-acceleration extensions; cloud providers (AWS Graviton) include.
- Quantum-resistant compression (post-2030 issue).

**Lesson**: in computing, occasionally a tool dominates by combining many engineering trade-offs well rather than excelling at one dimension. zstd + Linux + Wireshark + git all share this characteristic.

hints: What was it designed to replace?
slides.workedSolution: zstd combines: high ratio (close to xz at level 22); fast compression (5-10× gzip); very fast decompression (~1.5-2 GB/sec); excellent multi-thread; native dictionary support; permissive BSD license; streaming + random-access. Replaces gzip + xz + (partially) brotli. Adopted by: Linux kernel, Docker/OCI, ZFS, btrfs, Cloudflare, HuggingFace, most Linux distros. Yann Collet (Facebook) 2015; LZ77 + FSE/tANS entropy coding. Levels 1-22 span LZ4-to-xz performance.

question.question: Drag to estimate the compression ratio (input:output) of zstd default on typical English text.
question.explanation: zstd default (level 3) on English text: ~3-4× compression ratio (so 1 GB → ~250-330 MB). gzip default: ~3×. zstd at level 22: ~4-4.5× (similar to xz). Neural codecs: ~6-8× (close to entropy limit). For comparison: highly-redundant data (logs, code) can compress 5-10×; already-encoded binary data minimal compression; pre-compressed (JPEG, MP3) usually doesn't compress further.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why compression has become 'invisible infrastructure' — used everywhere but rarely noticed by end users.
question.rubric: Mentions: compression saves ~3-10× on storage + bandwidth without user awareness. Web: gzip + brotli auto-encode HTTP responses; browsers transparently decompress. CDN: AVIF/WebP/JPEG served automatically by content type + browser support. OS: filesystems (ZFS, btrfs, NTFS) transparently compress + decompress files. Cloud storage (S3, GCS): server-side compression; transparent retrieval. Databases (columnar): Parquet + ORC + ClickHouse highly compressed; queries transparent. Streaming services: Netflix/YouTube/Spotify deliver compressed audio/video; user sees only quality + buffering. Container images: Docker pulls compressed layers. Log aggregators: heavy compression for retention. Mobile networks: compression at multiple layers (codec, transport, encryption). Compression-aware caching + dedup. ML models: quantization is a form of compression. Concludes: compression is foundational utility; absence would crash bandwidth + storage by 5-10×; ubiquity is its measure of success.
